stage.title: A claim worth testing
stage.speaker: Archive keeper
stage.motivation: Our atlas will travel further than any of us. Before we trust its pages, make a testable question and a repeatable experiment.
stage.travelText: We collect the tools this collection needs from the places we have already visited. Everything else stays where we left it.

area.label: The traveling archive

things.label: Observation
things.description: Two otherwise similar pots appear to dry at different rates; the sunnier one seems drier.

things.label: Notebook
things.description: A blank record with spaces for time, conditions and what was actually observed.

things.label: Comparison
things.description: A side-by-side arrangement that makes similarities and differences inspectable.

things.label: Question
things.description: Does the sunnier pot lose water faster because of its light exposure? The question suggests a possible explanation without establishing it.

things.label: Prediction
things.description: Under otherwise matched conditions, the more brightly lit pot should lose more water if the proposed explanation is right.

things.label: Measuring scale
things.description: A scale whose reading can be checked before trusting a difference between pots.

things.label: Reference standard
things.description: A known reference used to detect an offset in the measuring device.

things.label: Repeated readings
things.description: Several measurements made under recorded conditions, including their fluctuations.

things.label: Variable
things.description: A quantity that can take different values; in the opening experiment it is light exposure.

things.label: Fixed conditions
things.description: The teaching setup holds pot size and starting water constant while changing light.

things.label: Experimental protocol
things.description: The written protocol says what will be compared, measured and recorded. It turns a private trick into a procedure another person can attempt.

things.label: Compass
things.description: A small magnetic needle in a case, with a position chart for recording its direction.

things.label: Enclosed current demonstrator
things.description: A recovered educational display with a visible wire path and recorded current-on/current-off observations. Its wiring is not a construction task.

things.label: Above-and-below observation cards
things.description: Two recorded views identify the compass position relative to the same wire; their orientation marks allow a fair comparison.

things.label: Bar magnet
things.description: A familiar magnet with marked ends, supplied with the museum teaching collection.

things.label: Coil and needle-meter display
things.description: A prepared educational display pairs a coil with a sensitive needle meter. Its recorded trials include approaching, resting and withdrawing a magnet.

things.label: Induction-ring replica
things.description: A museum replica shows two separate windings around an iron ring. A companion recording preserves the meter view.

things.label: Switch timing log
things.description: Time marks identify connection, an interval with current unchanged, and disconnection in the ring demonstration.

things.label: Hand-generator exhibit
things.description: An enclosed educational generator with a lamp and a recording of the handle turning and stopping. The curator asks for an explanation, not a wiring plan.

things.description: Encode source pairs00→0,01→10,10→110,11→111. No codeword starts another, so concatenated codewords remain decodable. The common00 pair gets one bit; rarer pairs cost two or three. The earlier single-bit repetition example is unchanged.

things.label: Compression scheme
things.description: Expected length is0.7×1 +0.1×2 +0.1×3 +0.1×3 =1.5 bits per source pair, versus2 bits without compression. This model gives a25% average reduction before error-control overhead, not a shorter encoding for every pair.

things.label: Reliable communication scheme
things.description: Compression and error control address different pressures: saving capacity and surviving noise. The scheme makes their assumptions explicit rather than promising perfect communication at no cost.

args: Targeted later-chapter trial from an authored checkpoint, not full-campaign play. I completed electricity stage 17 and communications stage 18, then stopped voluntarily at the chapter boundary. The initial compass/current, magnet/coil and ring/log pairings were obvious in a pleasant way. Preserving quiet readings and distinguishing change from mere magnetic presence made me want the generator payoff; the final mechanical-energy explanation felt earned. I stalled after making the change argument because I had overlooked compass plus bar magnet. Hints on the argument, wire comparison and generator all had no partners, which briefly felt like a dead end; a compass hint restored momentum, and the direction-map branch then made sense. Communications was less engaging mechanically: I tried adding redundancy to the encoded message before sending it, and tried applying correction to the corrupted transmission, but both were rejected. The accepted order felt like arranging teaching labels rather than actually protecting and repairing a message. The explicit prefix-code example and 1.5-versus-2-bit calculation were the strongest reward there. Familiar direct combinations were often satisfying, but repeated abstract combinations and repeated cautions started to feel routine. I am stopping because these two resolved exhibits are a satisfying session and the next replication title does not make me eager to start another chain, not because I am blocked or required to stop. Four hints, seven rejected drops, no undo or revisits in my fresh play. This is my logical-interface experience, not a claim about human players or visual/touch usability.
